```{ojs}
//| output: false
import {zeta, eta, li, primesUpTo, hardyZ, zerosZ, psiSteps, explicitPsi, gcd, linspace, MERTENS} from "./zeta.js"
KNOWN_ZEROS = [14.134725, 21.022040, 25.010858, 30.424876, 32.935062, 37.586178, 40.918719, 43.327073, 48.005151, 49.773832]
ZEROS = zerosZ(300)              // ~138 zeros on the critical line, computed live
PRIMES = Int32Array.from(primesUpTo(10000000))
function piCount(x) {            // number of primes <= x (binary search)
  let lo = 0, hi = PRIMES.length;
  while (lo < hi) { const m = (lo + hi) >> 1; if (PRIMES[m] <= x) lo = m + 1; else hi = m; }
  return lo;
}
fmt = (v, d = 4) => (Number.isFinite(v) ? v.toLocaleString(undefined, {maximumFractionDigits: d}) : "∞")
C = ({blue: "#1d3557", red: "#b4451f", gold: "#d99a1e", green: "#2a9d8f", gray: "#9aa0a6"})
STYLE = ({fontSize: "17px", background: "transparent"})
```

## Where we left off

::: {.fact}
**$p$-series test.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^{p}}$ **converges** if $p > 1$ and **diverges** if $p \le 1$.
:::

- $p=1$: the harmonic series $1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots$ diverges, even though its terms go to $0$.
- $p=2$: $1+\frac14+\frac19+\cdots$ converges. **To what?**

. . .

Today's goal: follow this one simple formula to one of the deepest open problems in mathematics. Along the way we'll discover

1. a famous number hiding in $\sum 1/k^2$,
2. why the $p$-series knows everything about **prime numbers**,
3. what the **Riemann Hypothesis** says, and why it's worth \$1,000,000.

## A new function is born

For every $p>1$ the series gives a number. Riemann named this function **zeta**:
$$
\zeta(p) \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k^{p}} \;=\; 1+\frac{1}{2^{p}}+\frac{1}{3^{p}}+\frac{1}{4^{p}}+\cdots,\qquad p>1.
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{ojs}
Plot.plot({

  x: {label: "p", domain: [1, 8]}, y: {label: "ζ(p)", domain: [0, 6], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([1], {stroke: C.gray, strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.ruleY([1], {stroke: C.gray, strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.line(linspace(1.17, 8, 400).map(p => ({p, z: zeta(p)})), {x: "p", y: "z", stroke: C.blue, strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.dot([2, 3, 4], {x: d => d, y: d => zeta(d), r: 6, fill: C.red}),
    Plot.text([2, 3, 4], {x: d => d, y: d => zeta(d), text: d => `ζ(${d})`, dx: 12, dy: -12, fontSize: 18, fill: C.red})
  ]
})
```

| $3$ | $1.2020569\ldots$ ??? |

## The Basel problem: where does $\pi$ come from?

- 1650: Mengoli asks for the exact value of $1+\frac14+\frac19+\frac1{16}+\cdots$
- The best mathematicians of Europe (including the Bernoulli brothers in **Basel**) fail.
- 1734: a 27-year-old **Leonhard Euler** shocks everyone:

$$
1+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{16}+\cdots \;=\; \frac{\pi^{2}}{6}.
$$

. . .

A sum of fractions of **whole numbers** produces $\pi$, the number of **circles**. Turn it around and compute $\pi$ from the $p$-series:

```{ojs}
viewof nB = Inputs.range([1, 100000], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "terms used", transform: Math.log, invert: Math.exp})
```

```{ojs}
{
  let s = 0; for (let k = 1; k <= nB; k++) s += 1 / (k * k);
  const est = Math.sqrt(6 * s);
  return html`<span class="readout">√(6·S<sub>${nB}</sub>) = ${est.toFixed(10)} &nbsp; vs &nbsp; π = ${Math.PI.toFixed(10)}</span>`;
}
```

## The key that opens the door to primes

Every whole number $> 1$ is a product of primes in exactly **one** way: $\;360 = 2^3\cdot 3^2 \cdot 5,\;\; 1001 = 7\cdot 11\cdot 13,\;\; 97 = 97.$

Now recall **geometric series** ($|r|<1$): $\;1+r+r^2+r^3+\cdots = \dfrac{1}{1-r}$. Take $r = \frac{1}{2^p}$ and $r=\frac{1}{3^p}$:

$$
\underbrace{\Big(1+\tfrac{1}{2^p}+\tfrac{1}{4^p}+\tfrac{1}{8^p}+\cdots\Big)}_{=\;1/(1-2^{-p})}
\underbrace{\Big(1+\tfrac{1}{3^p}+\tfrac{1}{9^p}+\cdots\Big)}_{=\;1/(1-3^{-p})}
= 1+\tfrac{1}{2^p}+\tfrac{1}{3^p}+\tfrac{1}{4^p}+\tfrac{1}{6^p}+\tfrac{1}{8^p}+\tfrac{1}{9^p}+\tfrac{1}{12^p}+\cdots
$$

. . .

Multiplying out gives each number built from 2s and 3s **exactly once** (unique factorization). Use **every** prime and you get **every** whole number:

::: {.big-idea}
**Euler's product formula (1737)**
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k^{p}} \;=\; \prod_{\text{primes } q}\frac{1}{1-q^{-p}}
\;=\;\frac{1}{1-2^{-p}}\cdot\frac{1}{1-3^{-p}}\cdot\frac{1}{1-5^{-p}}\cdot\frac{1}{1-7^{-p}}\cdots
$$
:::

## Euler's proof that primes never run out

Put $p = 1$ in Euler's formula:
$$
\underbrace{1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac14+\cdots}_{\text{harmonic series} \;=\; \infty}
\;=\; \frac{1}{1-\frac12}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\frac13}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\frac15}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\frac17}\cdots
$$

If there were only **finitely many** primes, the right side would be a finite product of finite numbers. But the left side is the **harmonic series, which diverges**. Contradiction!

::: {.big-idea}
The divergence of $\sum \frac1k$ (the $p=1$ case) **proves there are infinitely many primes**.
:::

```{ojs}
{
  const xs = [], ps = primesUpTo(5000);
  let prod = 1, H = 0, j = 0;
  for (let x = 1; x <= 5000; x++) {
    H += 1 / x;
    while (j < ps.length && ps[j] <= x) { prod /= (1 - 1 / ps[j]); j++; }
    if (x % 5 === 0 || x < 50) xs.push({x, H, prod});
  }
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 1100, height: 190, style: STYLE, marginLeft: 50,
    x: {type: "log", label: "x"}, y: {label: null, grid: true},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["∏ over primes q ≤ x of 1/(1−1/q)", "1 + 1/2 + … + 1/x"], range: [C.red, C.blue]},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(xs, {x: "x", y: "prod", stroke: () => "∏ over primes q ≤ x of 1/(1−1/q)", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.line(xs, {x: "x", y: "H", stroke: () => "1 + 1/2 + … + 1/x", strokeWidth: 2.5})
    ]
  });
}
```

## How many primes are there? More than squares!

Compare two series with "sparse" denominators:
$$
\sum \frac{1}{\text{squares}} = 1+\frac14+\frac19+\frac1{16}+\cdots = \frac{\pi^2}{6} \quad\textbf{converges}
\qquad
\sum \frac{1}{\text{primes}} = \frac12+\frac13+\frac15+\frac17+\frac1{11}+\cdots \quad\textbf{diverges!}
$$

(Euler again.) So, in the sense of series, primes are **more plentiful than perfect squares**, but the prime sum grows *incredibly* slowly, like $\ln(\ln x)$:

```{ojs}
{
  const ps = PRIMES, pts = [];
  let s = 0, next = 2;
  for (const q of ps) { s += 1 / q; if (q >= next) { pts.push({x: q, s, ll: Math.log(Math.log(q)) + MERTENS}); next = q * 1.05; } }
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 1100, height: 260, style: STYLE, marginLeft: 50,
    x: {type: "log", label: "add up 1/q for all primes q ≤ x"}, y: {label: "sum", grid: true},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["sum of 1/q", "ln(ln x) + 0.2615", "sum of 1/k² (squares)"], range: [C.blue, C.red, C.green]},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(pts, {x: "x", y: "s", stroke: () => "sum of 1/q", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.line(pts, {x: "x", y: "ll", stroke: () => "ln(ln x) + 0.2615", strokeDasharray: "6,4", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.ruleY([Math.PI ** 2 / 6], {stroke: () => "sum of 1/k² (squares)", strokeWidth: 2})
    ]
  });
}
```

[Using all primes up to ten million, the sum is still under 3. It reaches 4 only near $x\approx 2\times10^{18}$, and reaches 100 only when $x$ has about $10^{43}$ digits.]{.small}

## Bonus: $\pi$ hiding in pairs of random numbers

Pick two random whole numbers. What's the chance they share **no** common factor?

Chance they are **not** both divisible by 2 is $1-\frac{1}{2^2}$; by 3, $1-\frac{1}{3^2}$; by 5, $1-\frac{1}{5^2}$; … Multiply over all primes, and Euler's product **flips upside down**:
$$
P(\text{no common factor}) = \prod_{q}\Big(1-\frac{1}{q^{2}}\Big) = \frac{1}{\zeta(2)} = \frac{6}{\pi^{2}} \approx 60.8\%.
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

```{ojs}
  for (let a = 1; a <= N; a++) for (let b = 1; b <= N; b++) cells.push({a, b, c: gcd(a, b) === 1});
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 250, height: 250, style: STYLE, axis: null, margin: 2,
    marks: [Plot.cell(cells, {x: "a", y: "b", fill: d => d.c ? C.blue : "#e8e6e1", inset: 0.5})]
  });
}
```
[pairs $(a,b)$ up to 40; blue = no common factor]{.small}

```{ojs}
viewof nPairs = Inputs.range([100, 1000000], {value: 1000, step: 100, label: "random pairs", transform: Math.log, invert: Math.exp})
```

```{ojs}
  so π ≈ √(6 / fraction) = <b>${Math.sqrt(6 / f).toFixed(5)}</b><br>true π = ${Math.PI.toFixed(5)}</p>`;
}
```

## Counting primes: Gauss's discovery

Let $\pi(x)$ = **number of primes $\le x$** (just a name, nothing to do with $3.14$).

At age 15 (≈1792), Gauss studied tables of primes and noticed that near $x$, **about 1 in every $\ln x$ numbers is prime**. That suggests
$$
\pi(x) \approx \frac{x}{\ln x}
\qquad\text{or, better,}\qquad
\pi(x) \approx \operatorname{li}(x) = \int_0^x \frac{dt}{\ln t}\quad(\text{add up the densities}).
$$

```{ojs}
viewof logX = Inputs.range([1, 7], {value: 2, step: 0.05, label: "x = 10^"})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const X = Math.pow(10, logX), xs = linspace(2, X, 500);
  const data = xs.flatMap(x => [
    {x, y: piCount(x), s: "π(x), actual count"},
    {x, y: x / Math.log(x), s: "x / ln x"},
    {x, y: li(x), s: "li(x)"}
  ]);
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 1100, height: 270, style: STYLE, marginLeft: 70,
    x: {label: "x"}, y: {label: "number of primes", grid: true},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["π(x), actual count", "x / ln x", "li(x)"], range: [C.blue, C.gold, C.red]},
    marks: [Plot.line(data, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "s", strokeWidth: 2.5, curve: X < 200 ? "step-after" : "linear"})]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  const X = Math.pow(10, logX);
  return html`<span class="readout">x = ${fmt(Math.round(X), 0)} : &nbsp; π(x) = ${fmt(piCount(X), 0)}, &nbsp; x/ln x ≈ ${fmt(X / Math.log(X), 0)}, &nbsp; li(x) ≈ ${fmt(li(X), 0)}</span>`;
}
```

## The Prime Number Theorem (1896)

::: {.fact}
$$\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\pi(x)}{x/\ln x}=1.$$
Proved 100 years after Gauss's guess by **Hadamard** and **de la Vallée Poussin**, using Riemann's version of $\zeta$.
:::

| $x$ | $\pi(x)$ | $\operatorname{li}(x)$ | $\operatorname{li}(x)-\pi(x)$ | $\sqrt{x}$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $10^3$ | 168 | 178 | 10 | 32 |
| $10^6$ | 78,498 | 78,628 | 130 | 1,000 |
| $10^9$ | 50,847,534 | 50,849,235 | 1,701 | 31,623 |
| $10^{18}$ | 24,739,954,287,740,860 | 24,739,954,309,690,415 | 21,949,555 | $10^9$ |

. . .

::: {.big-idea}
The error is **tiny** next to $\pi(x)$: roughly $\sqrt{x}$ in size. **Is it always?** That question turns out to be the **Riemann Hypothesis**.
:::

## Are primes as random as coin flips?

A thought experiment (Cramér, 1936): build **fake primes**. Each number $n$ becomes a "prime" by a coin flip that lands heads with probability $1/\ln n$. Then compare the counting error, $\pi(x)-\operatorname{li}(x)$:

```{ojs}
viewof reroll2 = Inputs.button("New fake primes")
```

```{ojs}
{
  reroll2;
  const X = 1000000, M = 400, step = X / M, real = [], fake = [];
  for (let i = 1; i <= M; i++) { const x = i * step; real.push({x, e: piCount(x) - li(x), s: "real primes"}); }
  for (let r = 0; r < 3; r++) {
    let c = 0, next = step;
    for (let n = 3; n <= X; n++) {
      if (Math.random() < 1 / Math.log(n)) c++;
      if (n >= next) { fake.push({x: n, e: c - li(n), s: `fake primes #${r + 1}`, r}); next += step; }
    }
  }
  const band = linspace(2700, X, 300).map(x => ({x, hi: Math.sqrt(x) * Math.log(x) / (8 * Math.PI)}));
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 1100, height: 400, style: STYLE, marginLeft: 70,
    x: {label: "x"}, y: {label: "count − li(x)", grid: true},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["real primes", "fake primes #1", "fake primes #2", "fake primes #3"], range: [C.red, "#7aa6d6", "#9cc3a9", "#c9a6d6"]},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(band, {x: "x", y1: d => -d.hi, y2: "hi", fill: C.gold, fillOpacity: 0.15}),
      Plot.line(fake, {x: "x", y: "e", stroke: "s", z: "r", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      Plot.line(real, {x: "x", y: "e", stroke: "s", strokeWidth: 3.5}),
      Plot.ruleY([0])
    ]
  });
}
```

[Gold band: $\pm\frac{1}{8\pi}\sqrt{x}\,\ln x$. The real primes stay inside it *if and only if* the Riemann Hypothesis is true.]{.small}

## Part II · Riemann (1859): what if $p \le 1$?

**Bernhard Riemann** wrote just **one** paper on primes: *"On the number of primes less than a given magnitude"* (1859). His idea:

::: {.big-idea}
Make sense of $\zeta(p)$ for **every** $p$, not just $p>1$, and the primes will reveal their secrets.
:::

But wait: for $p\le 1$ the series $\sum 1/k^p$ **diverges**. How can $\zeta(p)$ have a value there?

. . .

**Trick: use an alternating series.** Flip every other sign:
$$
\eta(p) = 1-\frac{1}{2^p}+\frac{1}{3^p}-\frac{1}{4^p}+\cdots
$$
By the **alternating series test**, this converges for **every $p>0$**.

## Rescuing $\zeta$ with algebra

For $p>1$, subtract the two series:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\zeta(p)-\eta(p) &= 2\Big(\frac{1}{2^p}+\frac{1}{4^p}+\frac{1}{6^p}+\cdots\Big)
= \frac{2}{2^{p}}\Big(1+\frac{1}{2^p}+\frac{1}{3^p}+\cdots\Big) = 2^{1-p}\,\zeta(p)\\[4pt]
\Longrightarrow\quad \zeta(p) &= \frac{\eta(p)}{1-2^{1-p}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The right side makes sense for **all $p>0$** except $p=1$. So we **use it as the definition** of $\zeta(p)$ for $0<p<1$.

```{ojs}
viewof pH = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.95], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "p"})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const pts = []; let s = 0;
  for (let k = 1; k <= 60; k++) { s += (k % 2 ? 1 : -1) * Math.pow(k, -pH); pts.push({k, s}); }
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 1100, height: 155, style: STYLE, marginLeft: 60,
    x: {label: "terms of η(p)"}, y: {label: "partial sum", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(pts, {x: "k", y: "s", stroke: C.blue, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot(pts, {x: "k", y: "s", fill: C.blue, r: 3}),
      Plot.ruleY([eta(pH)], {stroke: C.red, strokeDasharray: "6,4", strokeWidth: 2})
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
html`<span class="readout">η(${pH.toFixed(2)}) = ${eta(pH).toFixed(6)} &nbsp; ⟹ &nbsp; ζ(${pH.toFixed(2)}) = ${zeta(pH).toFixed(6)}</span>`
```

[Even though $\sum 1/k^{p}$ diverges here, $\zeta(p)$ now has a value, and it's **negative**!]{.small}

## The whole graph of $\zeta(p)$

For $p\le 0$ Riemann found a **mirror formula** relating $\zeta(p)$ to $\zeta(1-p)$:
$$
\zeta(p) = 2^{p}\,\pi^{p-1}\,{\color{#b4451f}\sin\!\Big(\frac{\pi p}{2}\Big)}\,\Gamma(1-p)\,\zeta(1-p)
\qquad(\Gamma = \text{"factorial" for non-integers}).
$$
The sine is $0$ at $p=-2,-4,-6,\dots$, so $\zeta$ has **zeros** there (the *trivial zeros*).

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{ojs}
  return Plot.plot({

      Plot.dot([{p: 0, z: -0.5}, {p: -1, z: -1/12}, {p: 0.5, z: zeta(0.5)}], {x: "p", y: "z", r: 6, fill: C.red}),
      Plot.text([{p: 0, z: -0.5, t: "ζ(0) = −1/2"}, {p: -1, z: -1/12, t: "ζ(−1) = −1/12"}], {x: "p", y: "z", text: "t", dy: 24, fontSize: 16, fill: C.red})
    ]
  });
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{ojs}
{
  const d = linspace(-15, -0.5, 800).map(p => ({p, z: zeta(p)}));
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 560, height: 360, style: STYLE, marginLeft: 60, clip: true,
    x: {label: "p   (zoomed in on negative p)"}, y: {label: null, domain: [-0.1, 0.1], grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
      Plot.line(d.filter(d => Math.abs(d.z) < 0.2), {x: "p", y: "z", stroke: C.blue, strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.dot([-2, -4, -6, -8, -10, -12, -14], {x: d => d, y: 0, r: 6, fill: C.red})
    ]
  });
}
```
:::
::::

[About "$1+2+3+\cdots=-\frac{1}{12}$": that series **diverges** ($p=-1$). What's true is that Riemann's extended function has $\zeta(-1)=-\frac1{12}$.]{.small}

## Going 2D: inputs that are points

Riemann went further: he fed $\zeta$ inputs that are **points $(x,y)$ in the plane**. (The official language is *complex numbers*, but we can do it with arrows.)

::: {.fact}
For the point $(x,y)$, the term $\dfrac{1}{k^{p}}$ becomes an **arrow** of length $\dfrac{1}{k^{x}}$ turned by angle $y\ln k$.<br>
$\zeta(x,y)$ = where you land after placing all the arrows **tip to tail**.
:::

- When $y=0$ the arrows all point the same way: it's our old $p$-series with $p=x$.
- **Total length of the path** $=\sum 1/k^{x}$, which is a $p$-series! It's finite exactly when $x>1$.
- For $0<x\le 1$ we use the alternating version $\eta$ (flip every other arrow) and divide by $1-2^{1-p}$ as before.

. . .

::: {.big-idea}
A **zero** of $\zeta$ is a point $(x,y)$ where the arrow path ends **exactly back at the start**.
:::

## Hunt for a zero yourself

```{ojs}
viewof xA = Inputs.range([0.1, 1.5], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: "x"})
viewof yA = Inputs.range([0, 50], {value: 10, step: 0.001, label: "y"})
```

```{ojs}
yUse = yA
{
  const N = 3000, pts = [{k: 0, X: 0, Y: 0}];
  let X = 0, Y = 0;
  for (let k = 1; k <= N; k++) {
    const r = (k % 2 ? 1 : -1) * Math.pow(k, -xA), a = -yUse * Math.log(k);
    X += r * Math.cos(a); Y += r * Math.sin(a);
    pts.push({k, X, Y});
  }
  const end = {X: (pts[N].X + pts[N - 1].X) / 2, Y: (pts[N].Y + pts[N - 1].Y) / 2};
  const dist = Math.hypot(end.X, end.Y);
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: 760, height: 470, style: STYLE, aspectRatio: 1, inset: 10, marginLeft: 55,
    x: {label: null}, y: {label: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(pts.slice(0, 400), {x: "X", y: "Y", stroke: C.blue, strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      Plot.line(pts.slice(399), {x: "X", y: "Y", stroke: C.blue, strokeOpacity: 0.35}),
      Plot.dot([{X: 0, Y: 0}], {x: "X", y: "Y", r: 9, stroke: C.green, strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.dot([end], {x: "X", y: "Y", r: 6, fill: C.red}),
      Plot.text([{X: 0, Y: 0}], {x: "X", y: "Y", text: () => "start", dy: -18, fill: C.green, fontSize: 16})
    ]
  });
  return html`<div style="display:flex;gap:30px;align-items:center">${plot}
  <div style="font-size:0.7em">
  <p>Arrow k: length 1/k<sup>${xA.toFixed(2)}</sup>, turned by ${yUse.toFixed(3)}·ln k</p>
  <p class="readout">distance from end (red) to start (green):<br><b style="font-size:1.3em">${dist.toFixed(4)}</b></p>
  <p>${dist < 0.01 ? "🎯 <b>You found a zero!</b>" : "Type x = 0.5 and y = 14.1347 (or 21.0220, or 25.0109) in the boxes"}</p>
  <p class="muted">Then move x away from 0.5: the path never closes again.</p></div></div>`;
}
```

## The Riemann Hypothesis

```{ojs}
{
  const trivial = [-2, -4, -6, -8, -10, -12].map(x => ({x, y: 0}));
  const nontriv = ZEROS.filter(g => g < 60).flatMap(g => [{x: 0.5, y: g}, {x: 0.5, y: -g}]);
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 1150, height: 440, style: STYLE, marginLeft: 50,
    x: {domain: [-13, 4], label: "x"}, y: {domain: [-60, 60], label: "y", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.rect([{x1: 0, x2: 1, y1: -60, y2: 60}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: "y1", y2: "y2", fill: C.gold, fillOpacity: 0.18}),
      Plot.rect([{x1: 1, x2: 4, y1: -60, y2: 60}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: "y1", y2: "y2", fill: C.green, fillOpacity: 0.12}),
      Plot.ruleX([0.5], {stroke: C.red, strokeDasharray: "6,4"}),
      Plot.ruleY([0]), Plot.ruleX([0]),
      Plot.dot(trivial, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 6, fill: C.blue}),
      Plot.dot(nontriv, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 5, fill: C.red}),
      Plot.text([{x: 2.5, y: 50, t: "p-series converges\n(no zeros here)"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", fontSize: 16, fill: C.green}),
      Plot.text([{x: -7, y: 8, t: "trivial zeros  −2, −4, −6, …"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", fontSize: 16, fill: C.blue}),
      Plot.text([{x: 0.5, y: 63, t: "x = 1/2"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", fontSize: 16, fill: C.red, dy: 8})
    ]
  });
}
```

::: {.big-idea}
**Riemann Hypothesis (1859).** Apart from $-2,-4,-6,\dots$, every zero of $\zeta$ lies on the line $x = \tfrac12$.
:::

[More than 10 trillion zeros have been checked: all on the line. No proof. Since 2000 it's one of the Clay Institute's **\$1,000,000 Millennium Prize Problems**.]{.small}

## Walking up the line $x=\tfrac12$

On the critical line, the size of $\zeta$ is given by a **real** function built from **cosines and logs** (Riemann–Siegel):
$$
Z(y) \approx 2\sum_{k\le\sqrt{y/2\pi}} \frac{\cos\!\big(\theta(y) - y\ln k\big)}{\sqrt{k}},
\qquad \theta(y)\approx \frac{y}{2}\ln\frac{y}{2\pi}-\frac{y}{2}-\frac{\pi}{8}.
$$
Every time $Z$ crosses zero, we've found a zero of $\zeta$ **on the line**.

```{ojs}
viewof Ymax = Inputs.range([30, 300], {value: 60, step: 5, label: "walk up to y ="})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const d = linspace(9, Ymax, 2500).map(y => ({y, z: hardyZ(y)}));
  const zs = ZEROS.filter(g => g <= Ymax);
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 1150, height: 270, style: STYLE, marginLeft: 50,
    x: {label: "y (height on the line x = 1/2)"}, y: {label: "Z(y)", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
      Plot.line(d, {x: "y", y: "z", stroke: C.blue, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot(zs, {x: d => d, y: 0, r: 4, fill: C.red})
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
html`<span class="readout">${ZEROS.filter(g => g <= Ymax).length} zeros found up to height ${Ymax}, all on the line</span>`
```

## The music of the primes

Riemann's **explicit formula**: the zeros build the primes. Take a staircase that steps up by $\ln q$ at each prime $q$ (and prime power):
$$
\text{staircase}(x) = x \;-\; \sum_{\text{zeros } y} \frac{2\sqrt{x}\,\big(\tfrac12\cos(y\ln x) + y\sin(y\ln x)\big)}{\tfrac14+y^{2}} \;-\;\ln(2\pi)-\tfrac12\ln\!\big(1-x^{-2}\big)
$$
Each zero adds a **wave**: its height $y$ sets the **pitch**, and $\sqrt{x}$ (the $\tfrac12$ in $x=\tfrac12$!) sets the **volume**.

```{ojs}
viewof K = Inputs.range([0, ZEROS.length], {value: 0, step: 1, label: "number of zeros (waves) used"})
viewof Xm = Inputs.range([20, 150], {value: 50, step: 5, label: "x up to"})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const steps = psiSteps(Xm), zs = ZEROS.slice(0, K);
  const wave = linspace(2, Xm, 1500).map(x => ({x, y: explicitPsi(x, zs)}));
  const pr = primesUpTo(Xm);
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 1150, height: 205, style: STYLE, marginLeft: 50,
    x: {label: "x"}, y: {label: null, grid: true},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["prime staircase", `x + ${K} waves`], range: [C.blue, C.red]},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleX(pr, {stroke: C.gray, strokeOpacity: 0.35}),
      Plot.line(steps, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: () => "prime staircase", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.line(wave, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: () => `x + ${K} waves`, strokeWidth: 1.8})
    ]
  });
}
```

[Slide the number of zeros up: the smooth line $y=x$ grows sharp steps exactly at the primes (gray lines).]{.small}

## Why the line $x=\tfrac12$ matters

Each zero at $(x_0, y)$ adds a wave of size about $\text{(input)}^{x_0}$ to the prime count.

- All zeros on $x_0=\tfrac12$ $\Rightarrow$ every wave has size $\approx \sqrt{x}$ $\Rightarrow$ the **error in counting primes is as small as it can be**, like coin flips.
- A single zero at $x_0 = 0.7$ $\Rightarrow$ a wave of size $x^{0.7}$, much louder. The primes would be **less regular** than random.

::: {.big-idea}
$$\textbf{Riemann Hypothesis}\iff |\pi(x)-\operatorname{li}(x)| < \tfrac{1}{8\pi}\sqrt{x}\,\ln x \ \text{ for all } x\ge 2657.$$
"The primes are as evenly spread as they possibly could be."
:::

. . .

Why care? Prime numbers secure every online purchase (RSA encryption), and hundreds of theorems begin with *"Assuming the Riemann Hypothesis…"*.

## Breaking news (Oct 2026): an AI proves "quasi-RH"

Since 1896 we've known the nontrivial zeros sit in the strip $0 < x < 1$. The **quasi-Riemann Hypothesis**: prove they sit in some **narrower** strip.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}
- **Oct 6, 2026:** OpenAI released proofs written by an internal AI model:
  - 199 pages, **checked by computer (Lean)**: zeros have $\tfrac18 < x < \tfrac78$ (the stronger result)
  - a shorter 49-page proof of a slightly **wider** strip, $\tfrac1{12} < x < \tfrac{11}{12}$, easier for humans to check
- "the vast majority of consequences of RH already follow from quasi-RH" (M. Radziwiłł, NYU)
- **Still open:** are the zeros exactly on $x=\tfrac12$? The \$1M is unclaimed.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{ojs}
{
  const names = ["known (1896)", "AI, 49 pages", "AI, Lean-checked", "RH (open)"];
  const bands = [
    {x1: 0, x2: 1, a: "0", b: "1", c: C.gray},
    {x1: 1/12, x2: 11/12, a: "1/12", b: "11/12", c: C.green},
    {x1: 1/8, x2: 7/8, a: "1/8", b: "7/8", c: C.gold},
    {x1: 0.49, x2: 0.51, a: "", b: "½ only", c: C.red}
  ].map((d, i) => ({...d, y: names[i]}));
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 560, height: 300, style: STYLE, marginLeft: 150, marginRight: 30, marginBottom: 45,
    x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "x (real part of the zeros)", ticks: [0, 0.5, 1], tickFormat: d => ({0: "0", 0.5: "½", 1: "1"})[d]},
    y: {domain: names, label: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.barX(bands, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y: "y", fill: "c", fillOpacity: 0.8, insetTop: 10, insetBottom: 10}),
      Plot.text(bands, {x: "x1", y: "y", text: "a", dy: -22, fontSize: 14}),
      Plot.text(bands, {x: "x2", y: "y", text: "b", dy: -22, fontSize: 14}),
      Plot.ruleX([0.5], {stroke: C.red, strokeDasharray: "4,4"})
    ]
  });
}
```
[Where the zeros are allowed to be. Narrower strip = tighter control of the primes.]{.small}
:::
::::

[Source: Quanta Magazine, "AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now?" (Oct 19, 2026).]{.small}

## The whole journey

::: {.chain}
[$\sum \frac{1}{k^p}$: converges iff $p>1$]{.step} →
[$\zeta(p)$, with $\zeta(2)=\frac{\pi^2}{6}$]{.step} →
[geometric series + unique factorization]{.step} →
[Euler product $\prod \frac{1}{1-q^{-p}}$]{.step} →
[harmonic diverges ⇒ ∞ many primes]{.step} →
[counting primes: $\pi(x)\approx \operatorname{li}(x)$]{.step} →
[alternating series: $\zeta$ for $0<p<1$]{.step} →
[2D inputs: arrows]{.step} →
[zeros ↔ waves in the primes]{.step} →
[2026: AI proves quasi-RH, zeros in $\frac18<x<\frac78$]{.step} →
[**RH: all zeros on $x=\frac12$**]{.step}
:::
